title: What Parents?
author: Norma Sancho
summary: Norma Sancho, writing from a Mexican Gen X vantage point, reacts to a stream of news stories in which professors advise parents about AI and screens. Her argument is that the advice assumes parents exist who are able to guide children, when in her view many parents are as captured by digital habits as their kids. She faults Millennials and late Gen X for raising permissive children whose authority at home became, in her words, a bad joke. She contrasts this with her own childhood, where a poor grade carried real family consequences and parental authority was unquestioned. Her sharpest claim is that experts should address parents' own technology use and the parenting Gen Z received rather than adding another cautious note to a parenting column. The piece is a short, polemical opinion essay rather than research, but it frames the screen debate as a question about parental authority.
points: Sancho argues that screen-time advice for parents misses the root problem, which is that the adults themselves are absorbed in the same technology and are not positioned to supervise anyone.
She identifies permissive parenting and unconditional affirmation as a driver of instant-gratification habits in a generation now facing university and the job market.
The contrast between her strict, honor-driven upbringing and today's permissiveness frames parental authority as something that has been lost, not merely changed.
She calls for experts and journalists to turn the lens on parents' own device use rather than lecturing them about children's.
The essay is useful as a counter-cultural voice on the parenting side of the technology debate, and is best read as opinion rather than evidence.
quotes: Monitoring screen time? The content they consume? Hell, parents don’t even control their own. So, what game are the experts playing?
When are they going to address parents and their own use of technology? When are they going to talk about the kind of parenting Gen Z was subjected to?
Throughout their childhoods, these kids enjoyed a level of authority and permissiveness at home that turned parental authority into a bad joke.
They received “so much love” that they ended up receiving none at all—in the sense that they were “allowed to be themselves,” effectively cornered into the primitivism of instant gratification.
In Mexico, having a teacher say “your child doesn’t know how to read” came at a high price—a very high price.
It would be wonderfully insightful to simply acknowledge that “The Gen Z population has no mothers and no fathers... they have domestic friends”. And that’s it.
